turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi. Well, I'm here because I'm just having a really hard time with how I look lately. I can't stop seeing this... this droop and unevenness around my mouth and my jaw. I see it in every single photo and every time I catch my reflection. 

People keep telling me I look fine, but it feels so obvious to me. It's gotten to the point where it's really affecting my work. I'm an architect, and I've actually started avoiding giving presentations or meeting face-to-face with clients because I just don't want them looking at it.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient expresses persistent preoccupation with a perceived droop and asymmetry around their mouth and jaw, noting that others tell them they look fine.

turns.doctor_question: When you think about how you look, are you mainly worried about people noticing the asymmetry and judging you for it, or is it more that you feel the asymmetry itself is unacceptable no matter what others think?
turns.patient_response:
I'm not really sure. I haven't really thought about it that way before. 

I mean, I just know I can't stand it. I definitely don't want people looking at it, which is why I've been avoiding the presentations, but... I don't know if I'm more worried about them judging me or if I just hate it myself. It's hard to separate the two. I just know it looks wrong, and I really couldn't tell you which part of it bothers me more.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes intense distress and preoccupation with their perceived facial asymmetry, stating that they 'can't stand it', feel it 'looks wrong', and avoid presentations so people will not look at it.

turns.doctor_question: When you avoid giving presentations or meeting clients in person, is it more because you're worried they'll notice the asymmetry and think badly of you, or because you just can't stand how you look yourself, regardless of what they might think?
turns.patient_response:
I think... I mean, you kind of just asked me that, right? I'm really still not sure. 

It's just that when I have to stand up there in front of clients, I know they're looking right at my face. And I know the droop is there. I guess I just don't want them to see it. But whether it's because I think they're judging me or because I just hate knowing it's there on display... I really couldn't say. I just know I can't do it.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient expresses persistent concern and distress regarding a perceived facial 'droop' and extreme anxiety about others seeing it, consistent with preoccupation with an appearance defect.

turns.doctor_question: When you’re most upset about how your face looks, does the thought that others are noticing or judging it play the biggest role, or is it more about how you personally feel about how it looks, regardless of what others might think?
turns.patient_response:
Doctor, I... I feel like we're going in circles here. You've asked me this three times now. 

I really don't have a clear answer for you. I just know that I hate how my jaw looks, and I hate the idea of people staring at it when I'm trying to present my work. I can't pull apart whether it's my own disgust or my fear of their judgment that's driving it. It's just all tangled up together, and it's making my life miserable. I really don't know how else to explain it.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes persistent distress, self-disgust, and misery centered specifically on the perceived flaw in the appearance of their jaw.

turns.doctor_question: Can you think of a time when you were alone and not expecting anyone to see you — did you still feel just as upset about how your face looked then?
turns.patient_response: Yes, definitely. Even when I'm completely alone in my house, just working on some drafting or reading a book, it's still there. If I catch my reflection in a window or a mirror, it ruins my whole day. I don't need anyone else around to feel upset about it. It just looks wrong to me, and I can't stop focusing on it, even when there's no one else to see it.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes an inability to stop focusing on how their face 'looks wrong' even when completely alone, demonstrating persistent preoccupation with a perceived appearance flaw.

turns.doctor_question: Are you also concerned about any other parts of your body besides your face, or is it mainly the asymmetry around your mouth and jaw that troubles you?
turns.patient_response: No, it's really just my face. I mean, I have normal complaints like anyone else my age, I guess, but... nothing like this. It's just the jaw and the way my mouth droops. That's the only thing that actually consumes my thoughts and makes me feel this way. I don't really worry about the rest of my body.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient explicitly confirms that the perceived asymmetry and drooping around their jaw and mouth consumes their thoughts, reflecting a preoccupation with perceived facial defects.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself having repeated, intrusive thoughts about the asymmetry in your face, or do you feel driven to perform any specific behaviors—like checking mirrors, hiding your face, or seeking reassurance—because of it?
turns.patient_response:
Yes, I do. Before I go to work or to any family event, I can spend hours just checking the bathroom mirror. I'll take pictures on my phone from all different angles to see how bad it is, and I end up redoing my makeup and adjusting my scarf over and over again to try and fix it. 

I also ask my husband if my face looks lopsided... probably more than I should. And then I'll just sit there scrolling through photos of other women on my phone, comparing myself to see how bad my face looks next to theirs. So, yes, it definitely drives a lot of what I do.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient explicitly confirms engaging in repetitive behaviors related to appearance concerns, including spending hours checking mirrors, taking photos from different angles, excessively camouflaging with makeup and a scarf, seeking reassurance from her husband, and comparing herself to photos of other women.
